questiontext.text: Performing an in-order traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in what order?

feedback.text: Correct — in-order (left, root, right) on a BST yields keys sorted ascending.

answer.text: The order the keys were inserted

feedback.text: No — insertion order is not preserved by an in-order walk.
No — that would require visiting right before left.

answer.text: Level by level from the root

feedback.text: That is level-order, not in-order.

generalfeedback.text: Because a BST keeps smaller keys left and larger keys right, visiting left, root, then right produces keys in ascending sorted order.

questiontext.text: In a pre-order traversal, in what order is each node's work performed?

answer.text: Root, then left subtree, then right subtree

feedback.text: Correct — pre-order processes the root before its children.

answer.text: Left subtree, then root, then right subtree

feedback.text: That is in-order.

answer.text: Left subtree, then right subtree, then root

feedback.text: That is post-order.

answer.text: Right subtree, then root, then left subtree

feedback.text: That is reverse in-order, not pre-order.

generalfeedback.text: Pre-order = root, left, right. It is handy for copying a tree or printing a prefix expression.

questiontext.text: Which traversal visits the tree level by level and is naturally implemented with a queue?

feedback.text: Correct — enqueue the root, then repeatedly dequeue a node and enqueue its children.
No — recursive DFS uses the call stack, not a queue.
No — in-order is a depth-first order backed by a stack.
No — post-order is depth-first and uses a stack.

generalfeedback.text: Level-order / BFS uses a FIFO queue; the depth-first orders (pre/in/post) use the call stack or an explicit stack.

questiontext.text: Why is post-order traversal the right choice for freeing a tree or evaluating an expression tree?

answer.text: It processes both children before their parent

feedback.text: Correct — left, right, then root means children are handled before the node that owns them.

answer.text: It processes the parent before either child

feedback.text: That is pre-order, which would free a parent before its children.

answer.text: It visits nodes level by level

feedback.text: That is level-order, not post-order.
No — post-order visits every node, internal and leaf.

generalfeedback.text: Post-order = left, right, root. Handling children first lets you free their memory, or compute their values, before the parent needs them.

questiontext.text: An in-order traversal of a binary search tree outputs its keys in ascending sorted order.

feedback.text: Correct — left, root, right on a BST yields sorted keys.
It does — that is a defining property of a BST in-order walk.

questiontext.text: Level-order (breadth-first) traversal is naturally implemented with a stack.

feedback.text: No — a stack (LIFO) would give a depth-first order, not level-order.
Correct — level-order uses a FIFO queue; a stack would produce a depth-first traversal.

questiontext.text: Which depth-first traversal (name it) visits a BST's keys in ascending sorted order? Answer with the traversal name.

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about tree traversals are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Pre-order processes the root before its subtrees

feedback.text: Yes — pre-order is root, left, right.

answer.text: Post-order processes the root after both subtrees

feedback.text: Yes — post-order is left, right, root.

answer.text: In-order processes the root before its left subtree

feedback.text: No — in-order is left, root, right, so the left subtree comes first.

answer.text: Level-order is naturally implemented with a stack

feedback.text: No — level-order uses a queue.

generalfeedback.text: Pre = root/left/right, in = left/root/right, post = left/right/root. The DFS orders use a stack; level-order/BFS uses a queue.
